theme: The Noahic covenant; common grace; the rainbow sign
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 8:20-9:29 slowly. After the floodwaters recede, Noah disembarks and builds an altar. What follows is one of the most important covenant passages in the Old Testament, the Noahic Covenant, God’s pledge to preserve creation, and the rainbow as its sign. The chapter also ends on a sober note about Noah himself, reminding us that sin survived the flood.
settingTheScene:
After a year on the ark, Noah and his family emerge into a renewed world. Today’s reading covers what happens immediately after the flood, Noah’s first act of worship, God’s resolution never again to destroy the earth by water, the establishment of the Noahic Covenant, the institution of capital punishment for murder, the renewal of the dominion mandate, and a strange final episode involving Noah’s drunkenness and his sons.

The Noahic Covenant is one of the most important covenants in the Bible, but also one of the most misunderstood. It is not a covenant of salvation; it is a covenant of preservation. It is God’s commitment to maintain the natural order so that the larger story of redemption can unfold. Without the Noahic Covenant, there is no stable world in which Abraham can be called, Israel can be formed, or Christ can come. This covenant is the foundation of common grace, the kindness God shows to all people, not just to his chosen people.
observation: The first act after the flood is worship. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings.
God “smelled the pleasing aroma” and resolved in his heart never again to curse the ground because of man. The change is in God’s commitment to creation, not in humanity’s heart.
Verse 21 candidly admits: “the intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth.” Human nature has not been reset by the flood.
Verse 22 establishes the rhythm of creation: “seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease.” The natural world will be stable.
9:1 echoes Genesis 1:28: “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.” Humanity is given a new beginning.
9:6 grounds the prohibition of murder in the image of God: “whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image.”
The covenant is established with Noah AND with “every living creature”, it is universal in scope.
The rainbow is the sign of the covenant, a visible promise that judgment by water will not come again.
The chapter ends with Noah getting drunk, his nakedness exposed, and conflict among his sons, proving that human sin survived the flood.
interpretation:
The Noahic Covenant is one of the most theologically significant moments in the Old Testament, but it is often overlooked in favor of the more familiar covenants with Abraham, Moses, and David. Yet without the Noahic Covenant, none of those later covenants could exist. This is the covenant that holds the world together so that redemption can unfold within it.

Notice first how the section begins. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings. This is the first explicit act of sacrificial worship after the flood. Before God says anything about a covenant, before any blessing is given to the new humanity, Noah worships. And God responds. Verse 21 says, “When the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, the LORD said in his heart, “I will never again curse the ground because of man.”” The atoning sacrifice is not yet what it will be in Christ, but the principle is there: worship offered in faith elicits divine favor. God responds to sacrifice with promise.

And what a promise it is. Verse 21: “Neither will I ever again strike down every living creature as I have done. While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease.” This is God’s commitment to stability. The natural world will continue. The seasons will turn. The earth will produce food. Day will follow night. This is what theologians call common grace, the kindness God extends to the entire created order, both the righteous and the wicked, simply by sustaining the conditions of life.

Why does this matter? Because the verdict on humanity has not changed. Verse 21 admits it plainly: “the intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth.” The flood did not reset human nature. Noah and his family are not better than the people who died. They are saved by grace, not by superior virtue. And yet, despite humanity’s continued wickedness, God commits himself to preserving the world. Why? Because he is planning something larger. The flood was a temporary judgment that prefigured the final judgment to come. But before the final judgment can come, the story of redemption must unfold. The line of Seth must continue through Noah to Abraham. The nation of Israel must be formed. The prophets must speak. Christ must come. The gospel must spread to the nations. All of that requires a stable world, with seasons and harvests and history continuing. The Noahic Covenant is what makes that possible.

The covenant is then formally established in chapter 9. It has several distinctive features. First, it is universal. Verse 9 says God makes the covenant “with you and your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you”, every bird, animal, and human, present and future. Unlike the covenant with Abraham, which is particular to a specific people, this covenant is for all humanity and all creation. Every person who has ever lived, regardless of nation or religion, is a beneficiary of the Noahic Covenant. The food they eat, the seasons they enjoy, the air they breathe, these are gifts of common grace under this covenant.

Second, it includes the prohibition of murder, grounded in the image of God (9:6). This is the principle of the sanctity of human life. Whoever sheds human blood must answer for it, “for God made man in his own image.” The reasoning is theological, not pragmatic. Murder is not just a social crime; it is an attack on God’s image. This verse will become the foundation for all just systems of human government, the right to life, the responsibility to defend life, the establishment of justice systems to address violence.

Third, the covenant has a sign: the rainbow. “I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.” Every time it rains, the rainbow is meant to remind both God and humanity of this promise. Some scholars note that the Hebrew word for “bow” is the same word used for a weapon, and that God has “hung his bow” pointing upward, as if to say his weapon of judgment has been laid down. The rainbow is God’s commitment, written in the sky, that judgment by water is over.

Then comes the strange and sobering closing scene. Noah, the righteous one through whom humanity was preserved, gets drunk and lies naked in his tent. His son Ham sees him and apparently mocks him. His other sons cover him without looking. When Noah wakes, he curses Ham’s son Canaan. This passage has been misused throughout church history, especially to justify slavery and racism, interpretations that have no basis in the text. The point of the episode is simpler and more painful: sin survived the flood. Even the man through whom humanity was preserved is still a sinner. Drunkenness, family dysfunction, and curses all reappear in the very first generation after the flood. The flood washed away the world’s wickedness but not the wickedness in the human heart. A deeper solution will be needed.
connection: Yesterday we saw the flood as judgment and the ark as preservation. Today we see the covenant that follows: God’s commitment to maintain the world so that the story of redemption can unfold. The Noahic Covenant is the foundation of all common grace, every harvest, every season, every birth in every culture is a gift under this covenant. It is also the foundation on which the later covenants with Abraham, Moses, and David will be built. Without a stable world, there is no Israel, no land, no temple, no Bethlehem. And when Christ comes, he will fulfill not only the special covenants of grace but will reveal himself as the true Lord of the natural order, calming storms, multiplying food, raising the dead. The renewed creation that the Noahic Covenant points to will be fully realized in the new heavens and new earth.
application:
Today, recognize and respond to common grace. Every meal you eat, every breath you take, every sunrise you witness is a gift under the Noahic Covenant. God is patiently sustaining the world, including the parts of it that are still in rebellion against him, so that the gospel can reach more people, so that more sinners can be brought into the family of God. The reason your unbelieving neighbor’s garden grows is the same as why yours does: God’s faithfulness to the covenant he made with Noah.

This has practical implications. First, you can enjoy creation without guilt. The pleasures of food, music, beauty, friendship, work, these are gifts of common grace, given to all humanity, including you. Receive them with thanksgiving. Second, you can affirm what is good and true in the wider world without compromising your faith. When unbelievers do beautiful work, in art, science, justice, medicine, parenting, they are operating under common grace, and their work can be honored as such. Third, you can have hope for a world that often seems to be falling apart. The Noahic Covenant is still in force. God is still preserving creation. The story is not over.

And take seriously the dignity of human life. Genesis 9:6 grounds the sanctity of life in the image of God. Every human being you encounter, born and unborn, weak and strong, in your circle and outside it, bears that image. To diminish a human is to attack God’s image. To honor a human is to honor God. Today, look at the people around you with this conviction. Each one is a recipient of common grace, an image-bearer of God, a person for whom Christ died. Treat them accordingly.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for a gift of common grace that you rarely notice, such as the seasons, harvests, or order in the world.
Ask him to help you honor someone you meet today as an image bearer.
Thank him that his patience gives time for the gospel to reach people.
